chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
title: Playing Don Redman's booked dates when bookings ran short
summary: When bookings fell short, the band played dates sold as Don Redman's, with Redman waving the baton while they played their own book.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: We was speaking about the band carrying themselves. One time, the -- well, our bookings was running real short. So we took some dates that the little short guy, you know who I'm talking about, that arranged so -- you know, and he also used to write for the Chesterfield Band.
Yeah. You know who I'm talking about.
Little short fellow, was about that high, heck of arranger, wrote for the --
So what we would do, they booked dates for Don Redman's band and so my band would be playing today, see, and Don just stand up and --
-- use baton. Don would stand up and use the baton, you know.
So Don Redman's band, but he'd use the baton.

But it was so funny one night, the cat sounded so good. Some of the guys was talking about, 'Well, man, if something don't happen, we won't have to -- we have to try to get back home,' you know how guys --

Bird says, 'Man, listen. The way these cats played tonight, don't you worry about nothing. Ain't nobody going nowhere. There ain't nobody leaving here going nowhere and don't you even give it a whirl.'
Yeah, he said, "Yeah." I mean, the gas -- you know what I mean. "Ain't nobody going nowhere."
Did you play any of Don's arrangements or just your book?
No, we just played our book.
Uh-huh. Yeah, we just played our book
